headline: New moon springs load up the Shinnecock outgoing — night bass wake up, fluke slide to the inlet
subhead: Bigger tides and warm bay water are pushing everything toward the cut — the smart money's on the dark side of the clock this week.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay ran warm and sleepy — Shinnecock's been sitting up around the high 70s, same story as the Great South Bay to the west, and that kind of heat pushes fish out of the shallow flats and into anything with current and depth. Wind's been light out of the southwest most afternoons, which is fine for daytime boat traffic but does nothing for me. I do my work after the tourists go home. The moon's been drawing down toward new, and that's the piece that matters most going into this week — new-moon springs are building, and by Saturday through Monday (the 11th through the 13th) we'll have the biggest tidal exchange we've seen since before the last full moon. Bigger swing means more water moving through the inlet on the outgoing, which means bait gets flushed out of the bay in volume, and that's when the real fish show up to eat it.

Here's the mechanic I'm watching: the bay's warm, upper 70s, borderline uncomfortable for stripers and fluke that like it cooler. But right outside the inlet, upwelling has been dropping ocean temps into the low 70s — clean, cooler water sitting right on the other side of the jetty rocks. That temperature break is a wall, and everything that wants out of the warm bay stacks up against it on the ebb. It's the same read that's been pushing fluke out of the back bays and channels all along the South Shore this month, and Shinnecock's no exception. If you fish the inlet on a big outgoing this week, you're fishing the exact seam where warm bay water meets cool ocean water, and that's where the bait gets pinned and the predators get lazy about ambush spots.

Striper fishing at the inlet has been a night game, same as it's always been for me. I've had my best action working the outgoing starting about two hours before low, standing on the rocks or drifting the channel edge in the boat, throwing bunker spoons and darters along the north jetty where the current rips hardest. Fish have been mostly schoolies and mid-twenties, not the giants, but there've been enough slot fish in the 28-32 inch range mixed in to keep it interesting — three keeper-class fish out of maybe a dozen legit takes on a good outgoing, which is a fair night, not a great one. Live eels drifted on the bottom near the pilings under Ponquogue Bridge have also produced after dark, especially the last hour of the outgoing when the current slows enough for a natural presentation. It's not been lights-out. It's been honest work for a few solid fish a trip, and with the springs building toward the weekend I expect that current to get stronger and the bite window to get more concentrated — shorter but sharper.

Fluke have been the story everybody's talking about, and it's a real shift, not hype. The bay bite has gone quiet in the shallow sod banks and channels off Tiana — too warm, fish don't want to sit there. But the drift right in the inlet mouth and the deeper cuts leading out to the ocean side have turned on. Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and pink, 4-inch, on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through 15 to 25 feet of water on the last two hours of the outgoing — that's produced the better fish, several in the 3 to 5 pound range with a few doormats pushing 6 mixed in. The ocean side just outside the jetties, working that cooler upwelled water, has been the more consistent producer than the bay proper this week. If you're used to drifting the flats off Tiana Beach and it's been dead, that's why — the fish moved, they didn't disappear.

Weakfish at Ponquogue Bridge have been a mixed bag, which is about right for July. A few nice fish in the 3 to 5 pound class have come off the pilings on bucktails tipped with strips of squid, worked slow on the bottom during the last hour of the outgoing tide, same window as the bass. It's not the kind of consistent weakfish bite you could plan a whole trip around, but if you're already out there for bass or fluke, drop a bucktail near the structure and give it a few minutes — worth the five extra casts.

Bluefish have shown up in decent numbers chasing bait through the inlet on both tide changes, mostly cocktail-sized but enough teen-class fish mixed in to bend a rod. Poppers and metal on the surface during the last light hours have been the go-to, and they'll hit just about anything that moves fast.

The canal's been quiet for me this week — worth a look if you're running gear up to the Peconic side, but I haven't had the time to work it properly with the inlet doing what it's doing.

Looking ahead: Friday through Monday is the window. New-moon springs peak, the outgoing at Shinnecock Inlet will run harder than it has in weeks, and that cooler ocean water sitting outside the jetties should keep pulling bait and fish out of the warm bay. If I had one night this week, I'd be on the north jetty two hours before a big outgoing low, bunker spoon in hand, watching for the boils. Plan B is the fluke drift right in the inlet mouth on that same tide — either way, the moving water is doing the work. Just don't expect to sleep much.
